items.title: Which Branch Did My if Take? Seeing if / else if as a Flowchart
items.summary: In this series, we use JSVisualizer, a free browser-based tool, to understand classic algorithms by watching them run. The first post gave a tour of the tool, and the second looked at for loops. This time the topic is conditionals — if, else if, and else. The star of the show is the Control Flow view. This program turns a score into a letter grade: 80 or above is an A, 60 or above is a B, and anything lower is a C. let score = 72; let grade; if (score >= 80) { grade = "A"; } else if (score >= 60) { grade = "B"; } else { grade = "C"; } console.log(grade); It prints B. Short as it is, people who've just learned conditionals often wonder: When is the else if checked? 72 is "60 or above", so it's a B. But was the "80 or above" condition checked too? What about the else? Does the order of the conditions matter? What happens if you swap score >= 80 and score >= 60? Checking which branch ran is tedious. Plenty of us have sprinkled console.log("got here") into every block just to find out. JSVisualizer's Control Flow view turns your branches into a flowchart and shows, in different colors, the paths the program actually took and the ones it didn't. Isometric architecture diagrams are popular for a reason: a system drawn as zones and machines on a floor reads like a place, and people remember places. Most of them are made in drag-and-drop editors, though, and an exported PNG goes stale the week the system changes. Text-based tools such as Mermaid, D2 or Graphviz stay current but draw flat boxes. items.title: Ranking 1,700 AI tools by popularity with free data — Tranco + Chrome UX Report instead of SimilarWeb
items.summary: I run an AI tools directory with about 1,700 tools. Visitors want two things from it: which tools are actually popular, and which ones are taking off right now. For a while I scraped SimilarWeb for that. Then SimilarWeb started blocking my server's IP, and paying for their API wasn't an option for a side project. It turns out you can get surprisingly far with two free, public lists. This post shows the whole monthly job — about 100 lines of Node — and the traps I hit. items.title: Node.js Queue-to-Publish Design — Durable Alerts for Offline Fintech Users
items.summary: Presence should decide whether a fintech notification gets an immediate push, never whether the notification exists. Short answer: in a Node.js queue-and-publish service, commit each alert to a server-side inbox, enqueue its side effects, make one best-effort publish attempt for connected clients, and let offline users get notified by reading that inbox after reconnect. Keep read state on the server so a phone and a browser converge on the same answer. This gives you two viable system shapes. A durable-inbox design is the default for transaction alerts. A session-led design can be useful when the event belongs to a live advisory room and its artefacts must outlive that room. Neither design turns a realtime publish into durable storage. The bucket and object key identify the file; the returned URL is usable only within its expiration window. The deletion deadline belongs to the document record, not to the URL. Linux accounts can be configured to prevent password logins by replacing their password hash with an asterisk (*) in the /etc/shadow file. Because this is not a valid password hash, no password should allow access to those accounts. items.title: react-mobx-manager 4.6.0: persisting MobX stores without rewriting all of them
items.summary: Persistence in react-mobx-manager used to be simple and a bit wasteful. Every persisted store had a MobX reaction on toJS(store), and toJS walks every observable the store can reach, including other stores referenced from its fields. So a loading flag flipping in one store could make another store serialize itself again. Then every save wrote the whole storage value: one JSON blob holding all persisted stores. Version 4.6.0 (released 30 September, PR #53, promoted to latest in #54) reworks this. Short version: it saves less, and less often. The change listener tracks only the fields that are actually persisted. That is the union of the attributes you route to storages, or all exported fields when you use '*'. Stores referenced from those fields are no longer traversed. So if a persisted store also has short-lived fields, keep them out of storage. They stop causing persist work: import { Manager, makeExported } from '@lomray/react-mobx-manager'; export default Manager.persistStore(FeedStore, 'feed', { behaviour: 'include', attributes: { local: ['items', 'filters'] }, }); // or inside the store constructor makeExported(this, { isFetching: 'excluded' }); Stores that change within opti

items.summary: Originally published on Homingo Learn. Fear on a phone screen comes from where the camera stands and where the light falls. What each choice does, how to plan it shot by shot and how to build it for flat 2D art in code. Horror cinematographers work with a short list of tools: where the camera stands, how it moves, and which part of the frame the light is allowed to reach. An animated vertical Short uses the same tools, with two differences. The frame is tall and small, so every choice has to read at a glance on a phone. And there is no set: a camera move is a transform on your art layers, and a light is a layer you draw. This guide covers both halves, the film grammar and the code for it. Five heights, five meanings. Pick the height from who holds the power in the beat. The height of the camera decides who looks strong. That is the whole trick, and horror uses it in both directions: Overhead: the subject is pinned to the floor plan, small and watched. items.title: Return template
items.summary: Introduction A well-structured web application should keep presentation and application logic separate. The View should primarily describe the HTML structure, while server-side code handles data processing and application behavior. CodeBehind is a .NET Core framework built around this separation. Unlike approaches that embed server-side logic directly into HTML, CodeBehind provides mechanisms for keeping the View focused on presentation. However, loops and conditional statements can make this separation difficult to maintain. Consider a navigation menu generated from a collection of pages. In Razor, the implementation might look like this: @foreach (var page in Model.Pages) { @page.Title } Although this syntax is convenient, the View now contains both HTML and server-side control flow. Another approach is to generate the HTML entirely in the Controller: model.MenuHtml = " "; foreach (var page in pages) model.MenuHtml += $" {page.Title} "; model.MenuHtml += " "; This moves the logic out of the View, but makes HTML structures harder to read and maintain in server-side code. items.title: Working with templates in View
items.summary: Introduction As web applications grow, maintaining repeated HTML structures across multiple pages can become a challenge. Page headers, product cards, information panels, and other common elements often share the same markup. Copying these structures into every view increases duplication and makes future changes more difficult. CodeBehind addresses this through its Template system. It allows developers to define reusable sections of a page and insert them into other parts of the view. Templates can be defined directly inside a page or stored in external files. Both Razor Syntax and Standard Syntax are supported. Consider an online store where several pages display product information using the same HTML structure. Instead of repeating the markup for every product, we can define a template named ProductCard. Here is an example using Razor Syntax: @#ProductCard{ @model.ProductName @model.ProductDescription @model.ProductPrice } The template can then be referenced wherever its content is needed: @#ProductCard When CodeBehind processes the page, the template reference is replaced with the content defined in ProductCard. Employees are also being encouraged to use cheaper models or on-device AI. MacRumors reports: Engineers at Apple have the largest budgets because using AI for coding can consume a large number of tokens. Apple lets employees use Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and other models. Some Apple employees told Bloomberg that few were using their full $300 daily limit, so the savings may be small. Apple has also hired outside productivity consultants for some divisions. Combined with the AI cost cuts, the reviews have fueled worries about possible restructuring. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Building a browser metronome that stays in time at 1000 BPM
items.summary: I play fast music, and most metronomes I tried stop at 240 or 300 BPM. So I built one that goes to 1000: Unlimited Metronome. It is free, needs no account and works offline. This post is about the parts that turned out to be harder than "play a click every N milliseconds". setInterval is not a metronome The obvious version is a timer that plays a sound on every tick. It sounds fine at 80 BPM and falls apart as soon as anything else happens on the page: timers drift, the main thread is busy rendering, and browsers throttle timers in background tabs to once a second or less. At 260 BPM a beat is 230 ms long, so even a 20 ms wobble is audible. The fix is the pattern from Chris Wilson's article "A Tale of Two Clocks": keep two clocks with different jobs. A coarse JavaScript timer wakes up every 25 ms. It never plays anything itself. items.title: Mining 14,351 Chess Puzzles with Stockfish 18 (and the Illegal-FEN Trap in chess.js)
items.summary: When we started building Brass Pawn (source on GitHub, AGPLv3), we needed a large offline tactics, positional judgement, and endgame dataset that ran completely on-device—both in the browser and natively on iPhone, iPad, and Mac. Transcribing chess puzzles by hand or scraping unverified problem collections breaks down fast. Two failure modes show up immediately in real training: Cooked solutions: A position has a flashy sacrifice, so a human annotator marks it as winning—missing a quiet defensive resource at depth 18, or missing a second equally winning move that punishes a student for playing an objectively strong alternative. Horizon flips: A shallow engine pass (depth 10–12) flags a move as +2.10, only for depth 22 to reveal perpetual check (0.00). Instead of transcribing puzzles, we built a deterministic mining and independent verification pipeline powered by Stockfish 18. Along the way, we hit a subtle FEN validation edge case in chess.js that silently breaks UCI engines. A good tactics puzzle isn't simply "someone blundered in a game." items.title: Building Subscriptions Without Storing a Single Card Number
items.summary: We just added recurring product subscriptions to StoreFlux (a headless commerce backend), and the design decision I want to write about is the one that felt obvious in hindsight but wasn't the first thing I reached for: we don't store a customer's card at all. The "normal" way to build subscriptions is to tokenize the customer's card on the gateway (Stripe customer + payment method, say), save that token, and on each billing date fire an off-session charge against it. That's a completely reasonable design. It's also one most commerce platforms already have sitting around, because it's the obvious answer. I didn't want to build that, for a fairly unglamorous reason: it's a second payment path. Checkout already has a payment path — tested, handles declines, handles 3D Secure challenges, handles webhooks, handles every gateway-specific weirdness we've already run into. A separate off-session billing path duplicates all of that, badly, because off-session charges can't show the customer a 3DS challenge if one gets triggered. items.title: The React Illusion: Why the Industry's Go-To Library Is Full of Hidden Friction
items.summary: Over a decade ago, frontend development was trapped in a cycle of manual DOM tracking and fragmented state. The introduction of React in 2013 shifted that paradigm. Before React, most applications leaned on libraries like jQuery. Developers wrote imperative, step-by-step instructions to find an HTML element, update its text, append a child, and manually keep the data layer in sync with the browser. As applications grew, this approach turned codebases into fragile "spaghetti code," where changing a single button could silently break an unrelated form elsewhere on the page. Declarative data binding already existed in AngularJS and Knockout, but React reframed the problem. It treated the UI as a function of state: you describe what the screen should look like for the current data, compose it from small components, and let data flow in one direction. React handles the DOM updates under the hood. Compared to the heavyweight MVC-style architecture of AngularJS and early enterprise frameworks, React felt lightweight, predictable, and simple to write. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder's web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016. The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period. The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into "free" mobile and desktop applications. items.title: Discord Is Ditching Electron For Rust
items.summary: Discord is replacing Electron with a desktop client built fully in Rust, which the company says should significantly reduce the app's notoriously high resource usage while improving performance and memory safety. "We've been early adopters of Rust since 2018 and a lot of our infra, voice tech, and even some of the current client is already Rust, the holy grail was getting the whole client there," explains Discord chief technology officer Stanislav Vishnevskiy in a post on X. "That means Electron goes away, and so does React Native, mobile keeps native UI but shares app code with desktop via Rust." The Verge reports: Vishnevskiy also shared an image of the Discord Windows client using just 290MB of RAM, which is a clear improvement as you only have to participate in a few servers and RAM usage can easily hit 1GB or more using the current Windows app. It's not clear when Discord will make the full switch over to Rust, but Vishnevskiy says the company "hope to get it into testing with users soon." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.summary: I run a site with practice exams for Dutch certification exams. Each exam has a few fixed practice forms, at URLs like /examen/b-vca/1/, /examen/b-vca/2/ and so on. According to Motorola, the EVS action sensor (telephoto camera) is the first in a smartphone, offering "new possibilities for photographing moving subjects and captures even fast movement with impressive clarity and precision." items.title: Launch HN: Rivet (YC W23) – Scale and Orchestrate Agents on S3
items.summary: Hey HN, this is Nathan and Nicholas from Rivet (https://rivet.dev) – a fast, high-density, and scalable orchestrator for agentic workloads using the actor model. Rather than running a heavyweight sandbox per agent, each agent gets a lightweight actor backed by S3. Actors provide a long-lived process for long agent turns, in-memory state for context, a WebSocket server for multiplayer, durable SQLite storage backed by S3, and hibernation when idle. It's a similar model to Cloudflare Durable Objects, but it’s open source and self-hostable. Here’s a video walkthrough: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3Ev6I7DOV9c When we went through YC in 2023, we were building infrastructure for multiplayer games like Diep and Krunker. This involved heavily optimizing high-throughput matchmaking, real-time player messages, and blitz scaling. Through that process, we spent a lot of time on workloads where Postgres couldn't keep up with our throughput. We started out by hacking together Lua scripts on top of Redis, but this became too cumbersome to maintain and upgrade. items.title: Making a SwiftUI app survive a folding iPhone: what broke on the iPhone Duo and how I fixed it
items.summary: I make PawLife, a small pet health app (feeding plans in grams, a health diary, a food safety lookup). It is one SwiftUI codebase for iPhone, iPad, Mac Catalyst, Apple Watch and visionOS. When Xcode 27.2 shipped simulators for the iPhone Duo, I expected "it is just a wider iPhone". It is not. Here is what actually broke, in the order I found it, and what the fixes looked like. The Duo has an outer display and an inner one across the fold. Your app runs on one of them at a time, and the window changes size when the user folds or unfolds. The simulator reports it as a window resize, not a new scene. Measured on the simulator: Folded: a 466×678 pt window, of which my app got 382 pt of width. The remaining 84 pt on the trailing edge is a reserved column (status area and camera) exposed through the safe area. Open: a landscape 951×669 pt window, 867 pt for the app, with the same 84 pt trailing column. So the app goes from a narrow portrait phone to a wide landscape slab and back, live, without a relaunch. items.title: LISTEN/NOTIFY performance in PostgreSQL
items.summary: I'm building Corfedo Work, a .NET library for background jobs that keeps its state in the application's own PostgreSQL database. Its workers need to know when something changed: a job became due, or a job somebody is waiting for has ended. The PostgreSQL answer is NOTIFY in the transaction that made the change. I designed the library's signals around it. Then I measured it. Single-row transactions with a NOTIFY committed about 3,900 times per second with 8 clients, and about 3,900 with 64. Without the NOTIFY, the same transactions reached 16,700 and 56,700. A signal in Work says "something you wait for may have changed, read again". It's a topic and a key, with no data. items.title: Building PurpleWallet: a full-stack fintech app with a real ledger, AI, and ₦0 hosting
items.summary: PurpleWallet started as a backend exercise: a Node.js wallet API with Prisma, Redis and a few queues. items.title: Laravel CORS Error with React or Vue: Causes and Fixes
items.summary: You split the project in two: Laravel serves an API on localhost:8000, and a React or Vue app runs on localhost:5173. The first request from the browser fails, and the console shows a message along these lines (Chrome's wording): Access to fetch at 'http://localhost:8000/api/users' from origin 'http://localhost:5173' has been blocked by CORS policy: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource. The API itself is usually fine. CORS is a browser rule: the browser asks the server whether a page from another origin may read its response, and the server answers with headers. Laravel already has the machinery for that answer. Most fixes are a few lines of config, and I checked each one against the real middleware. Two URLs have the same origin only if scheme, host and port all match. localhost:5173 and localhost:8000 differ in the port, so every request between them is cross-origin. The server never blocks anything. It sends Access-Control-* headers, and the browser decides whether your JavaScript may see the response. items.summary: Processing PDFs entirely on the client side is becoming the gold standard for modern web applications. It provides zero-latency interactions, eliminates expensive backend compute (no headless Chrome or Ghostscript clusters), and guarantees 100% data privacy since documents never leave the user's browser sandbox. However, once you move from toy examples to handling real-world 50MB+ PDFs, you inevitably encounter three major bottlenecks: Silent Memory Leaks: Generating visual thumbnails in easily spikes tab memory past 1.5GB, crashing mobile and low-spec machines. Text Degradation: Many naive implementations convert pages into raster images, causing selectable vector glyphs to turn into blurry bitmaps. Strict Binary Parser Failures: pdf-lib is brilliant for lossless stream operations, but it strictly enforces PDF standards. When a user uploads a slightly malformed or non-compliant document, it throws Error: Expected instance of PDFDict, breaking the workflow. items.title: Understanding SwiftUI's layoutPriority: HStack, ZStack, and Custom Layouts
items.summary: SwiftUI makes building interfaces straightforward, but its layout system can sometimes produce unexpected results. One modifier that developers often reach for is .layoutPriority(). For example: swift This can help resolve layout issues, but what exactly does the priority value mean? And does the modifier behave the same way in every container? To explore these questions, I built an interactive open-source project called SwiftUI Layout Lab. The .layoutPriority() modifier provides a priority value that parent layouts can use when determining how to size their children. The default priority is 0. A higher priority doesn't directly specify a width, height, or percentage of available space. Its effect depends on the parent layout algorithm and the sizing behavior of the child views. For example, assigning a priority of 100 doesn't mean a view will receive 100 times more space than a view with priority 1. An HStack arranges views horizontally, but what happens when there isn't enough space for every view to receive its preferred width? In Layout Lab, you can: Select one of three views. Change its layout priority. Adjust the available container width. Observe the actual measured widths.

items.title: A Claude Client in One C# File, Compiled Ahead of Time
items.summary: Last week's client was Go: a 5.8 MB static binary that starts in under two milliseconds, which is a high bar for any language with HTTP in its standard library. This week it's C#. .NET has had everything the spec needs in the box for a decade, and since .NET 8 it has had Native AOT, which compiles the whole program to a single native executable with no runtime to install. I wanted to know whether that gets a C# client anywhere near Go on size and cold start. It gets closer than I expected, though the runtime column on the leaderboard shows what the binary size leaves out. The code is at github.com/AndyCross/claude-hot-path, and the spec every client passes is at /claude-hot-path/. The idiomatic way to do JSON in AOT .NET is System.Text.Json with a source-generated JsonSerializerContext, so the serialiser knows every type at compile time and nothing needs reflection. For a client this small I went the other way and used JsonNode, the DOM API, because the request body and the event payloads are built and read dynamically anyway and a context class would have doubled the file. items.title: I Changed object to Lock and Stopped Paying the Monitor Tax
items.summary: I had a counter behind a lock that a profiler kept flagging, and I couldn't figure out why. The lock was basically never contended. One thread wrote to it almost all the time; the lock was there for the rare second writer that might show up. So I expected it to cost close to nothing. It didn't cost nothing. It cost about 24 nanoseconds every single acquire, and on a hot path that adds up to a line you can see in a flame graph. The thing I'd stopped thinking about is what lock (someObject) actually compiles to. It's Monitor.Enter and Monitor.Exit wrapped in a try/finally, and Monitor hangs its state off the object's sync block. Even with no contention at all, you pay for that bookkeeping on every acquire and release. For years that was just the price of the lock keyword and there was nothing to do about it. Since .NET 9 there is. There's a real type now, System.Threading.Lock, and the compiler special-cases it: if you lock on a variable whose type is Lock, it doesn't go through Monitor at all. It calls the type's own fast path instead. The part that surprised me is how little the code changes. // before private readonly object _gate = new(); lock (_gate) { _count++; } // after priva

items.title: Crop Once, Post Everywhere: Batch Aspect-Ratio Crops for Social Images in Swift
items.summary: If you ship photos from an iPhone app to more than one place, you eventually hit the same boring problem: Instagram wants 1:1 or 4:5, a shop banner wants 16:9, Stories want 9:16, and the camera roll is full of 4:3 and 3:4 stills. Doing that crop by hand for thirty product shots is how afternoons disappear. This post walks through a small UIKit pipeline that takes one UIImage, a list of target aspect ratios, and returns one centre-weighted crop per ratio — suitable for running across a whole album. I’m writing it from the seat of someone who builds BatchMark, an on-device batch photo app, where “apply the same finishing step to many photos” is the whole product. The code below is a teaching extract, not a dump of the app. People say “crop to 1:1” and mean two different things: Aspect-fill crop: keep the photo’s resolution as high as possible, cut off the edges that don’t fit the ratio. Aspect-fit pad: show the whole photo, add bars (or a mat) to reach the ratio. For social uploads you almost always want (1). items.summary: I'm building yabbistir, a clipboard history for macOS. Its one trick is where it opens: press ⇧⌘V and the panel appears 8 points under the text caret of whatever app you're typing in. You type to search, press ↵, and the item is pasted back into that app. Your eyes don't travel and your hands don't leave the keyboard. That needs three things macOS doesn't hand you directly: the caret's position in someone else's app, a sensible answer when that app won't tell you, a window that takes keystrokes without taking focus away from the app you're typing in. Here is how each one works, with code from the app, shortened. There's no "where is the caret" API on macOS. There is the Accessibility API, the one assistive apps like VoiceOver use to read other apps' interfaces. Your app needs the Accessibility permission for it (AXIsProcessTrusted() tells you whether you have it), and then it can ask three questions: Which element has keyboard focus? Ask the system-wide element for kAXFocusedUIElementAttribute. What's selected in it? kAXSelectedTextRangeAttribute returns a CFRange. With nothing selected, it's an empty range at the caret. items.title: Cleaning duplicate photos inside Lightroom Classic and Capture One catalogs without breaking them
items.summary: Disclosure: I'm the developer of Folio Refresh, the Mac app this post is about. Most duplicate photo finders work on folders. Point them at a drive, they hash files, they move copies to the Trash. That is fine until the photos live in a Lightroom Classic or Capture One catalog. Delete a file behind Lightroom's back and the catalog shows a missing-photo badge; delete the wrong copy and you lose the edits, ratings and collections attached to it. When I built Folio Refresh I wanted it to clean duplicates inside those catalogs, so here is how it does that without corrupting them. A Lightroom Classic catalog (.lrcat) is a SQLite database. A Capture One catalog (.cocatalog) is a package with a SQLite database (.cocatalogdb) inside. Neither schema is documented, and both change between versions. That shapes every rule below. Scanning only ever opens the catalog read-only. Lightroom: SQLITE_OPEN_READONLY. SQLite guarantees a read-only connection cannot write the database or its log, so this is safe even while Lightroom has the catalog open; it is just another reader. items.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time review – a dream come true
items.summary: Nintendo Switch 2; Nintendo This ambitious remake transforms a landmark Zelda game into a modern masterpiece, clearer and easier to navigate, more beautiful to look at, with playful musical touches. Yet the melancholy remains It’s always a worry, returning to a formative piece of art from your childhood. Will your jaded adult sensibilities render you unable to locate the magic that captivated your child self? Will revisiting it reveal that it was never actually that good, and that your tastes are built on a foundation of lies? With video games, there is the added complication of technological advancement: decades-old games can look so basic and feel so treacly to play that it’s hard to explain why they were mind-blowing at the time. Light-touch remasters aim to bring such games up to modern graphical standards without fundamentally changing them; an ambitious remake attempts to transform the work into something that can stand alongside any modern masterpiece. Ocarina of Time is the latter. And I could not be more delighted to report that it is a dream come true. Continue reading...

items.title: How the Claude Code team does code review (18 minute read)
items.summary: Claude writes about 90% of the code in Claude Code. This post explains how the team reviews the code at the volume its agents produce. The team moved most of the reading in the review stage to machines, optimized for human time and attention, and invested heavily in making it fast and easy to undo mistakes. This resulted in merged pull requests to Claude Code's codebase more than doubling while the share that had to be reverted fell by more than 40% between June and September.

items.title: The Biggest Takeaways From Anthropic's IPO Prospectus (8 minute read)
items.summary: Anthropic unveiled its IPO paperwork yesterday, putting it on track to go public as soon as the week before Thanksgiving. The 400-page prospectus tells a story of how the company could usher in a new era of progress that will transform how people code, conduct research, build financial models, and automate routine tasks. It also warned that AI could lead to the development of new bioweapons, destabilize the geopolitical order, and evolve beyond the ability of humans to understand and control. Anthropic plans to trade on the NASDAQ under the ticker 'ANT', with a valuation expected to land between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion.

items.title: Working with academic communities to build scientific understanding (12 minute read)
items.summary: OpenAI has announced three new discoveries in mathematics, computer science, and physics. For the math result, which is about harmonic analysis, the AI lab will release the AI output, so researchers are free to organize their own efforts to explain the result. OpenAI will form an external group of collaborators to explain the computer science result, which is about complexity theory, and will make the AI output publicly available. The lab will also form an external group of collaborators for the physics result, which is about quantum field theory, but defer to them on the release of the materials.

items.title: Is a job guarantee the solution to mass AI unemployment?
items.summary: An old idea springs anew as a chorus of influential voices predicts that AI may trigger crises of vast magnitude In a preface to his book Capitalism and Freedom, the American economist Milton Friedman famously observed that a crisis can propel once-fringe ideas into the political mainstream. “Only a crisis – actual or perceived – produces real change. When that crisis occurs, the actions that are taken depend on the ideas that are lying around,” he wrote. The job of intellectuals, thinktanks and economists, he argued, is to refine the quality of these ambient ideas, so that good ones are ready when disaster strikes. Continue reading...

items.title: I’m a CTO. AI still needs your human expertise | Madhu Shashanka
items.summary: AI is increasingly getting good at doing some tasks, but it can never replace human workers’ judgment Autonomous cars, which may be the safest we have built, keep getting easily avoidable parking tickets. While Waymos crash far less often than human drivers over tens of millions of miles, they’re still terrible at performing basic tasks – keeping out of disabled parking spots and tow-away zones, or steering clear of a church garage during Sunday service, according to the Wall Street Journal. That is the state of AI today: impressively capable at something complex, yet embarrassingly clumsy at something easy. And it has implications for what work will remain human and what will be automated by AI. Madhu Shashanka is co-founder, chief scientist and chief technology officer at Concentric AI, a data security software company Continue reading...
